div.p: Philodryas baroni (Baron's Green Racer) and Trimorphodon lambda (Sonoran Lyre Snake) each belong to extensively studied genera of rear-fanged venomous snakes. Investigating the bioactivities and structural composition through methods not typically included in venomic workflows, which use homologous sequences and describe venoms by their constituent peptides, provides valuable insights into both the degree and extent to which venom diversity and complexity can be overlooked by many venomic workflows. This study explores the venom compositions of P. baroni and T. lambda and compares them to published toxins observed in opisthoglyphous snakes, specifically taxon-selective three-finger toxins and metalloproteasedominated venoms.

This study underscores a greater degree of quaternary structure variability within previously sequenced and described rear fanged snake venoms. This variability also occurs in tandem with shifts in potency and specificity characteristics of the toxins described.
Characteristics desirable when searching for translatable mechanisms capable of altering characteristics of existing proteins or synthetic peptide therapeutics in favorable directions.

div.head: Background
div.p: Bioprospecting can be defined to sound exploitative, dangerous, or miraculous, but at its core it is simply the research of natural biodiversity of any kind that is funded, motivated, presented as, or effectively produces an innovation with social and/or commercial value.

Pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, agriculture, nanotechnology and biomimetic engineering encompass a massive variety of applications of natural materials that may be heavily reliant on farming or collection of natural materials, while others are inspired by the diversity of naturally occurring bioactive substances that are effective at relieving symptoms of, or even treating, diseases and pathologies (Beattie et al., 2011). Although we have been mining for minerals deep in the earth for centuries, only in our most recent history have we been able to understand and anticipate, isolate and repurpose the nearly limitless diversity of bioactivities present in the natural world (Das, 2020). Fever-reducing teas and natural remedies date back millennia in some regions and are nearly ubiquitous with long-term human occupation in a region. However, until more recently, humanity lacked the tools to isolate compounds (such as proteins) from one another from complex heterogenous mixtures (Beattie et al., 2011). Once the effective isolation of proteins and protein complexes was possible, the high structural variability and diverse range of bioactivities made toxins and their natural sources an obvious target for bioprospecting for novel compounds with pharmaceutical, cosmetic and biotechnological utility (Rayan et al., 2017). Takacs (2021) defined venom as the mixture of molecules secreted and delivered through a traumatic perforation by a venomous organism to deleteriously impact the physiological capabilities of an envenomated organism. Takacs succinctly defined venoms with an emphasis on the ecological role and delivery of a sufficient amount to perform that role. An alternative definition of venom by Schendel et al. (2019) defined it as a biochemical arsenal containing bioactive mixtures of salts, small molecules and proteins (including small peptides) that function as toxins (therefore deleterious) by synergistically or individually targeting components essential to normal physiological and signaling processes, usually with great potency. This definition, unlike Takacs, came from a review of not just reptile venoms, but of venoms from any of the approximately 100 animal lineages thought to have undergone convergent evolution to deliver toxins directly into another organism. Among this diversity come more obvious applications of venom in various roles unrelated to the organism. As the research presented in this thesis is not concerned with platypus or cephalopods, nor applications including conspecific disputes over territory, mating, antimicrobial ointment, or long-term prey storage, the definition offered by

Takacs is far more apt. While seemingly semantic, properly qualifying the requirements that define a venomous condition is extremely important for anyone studying venom from ecological, evolutionary, and bioprospecting perspectives. Schendel et al. (2019) specifically elaborated on one area where the term venoms can be misleading when considered a protein produced by an organism for that same organism.

Specifically, they emphasized that venom proteins are an inherently difficult model to use for evolutionary studies compared to endogenous mutations in essential components of normal physiological functions. One potentially misleading conclusion is mistaking the loss of a prior mechanism and reduced toxicity as a loss of function, whereas if a different model organism was used one would assume, also incorrectly, it had gained affinity for its target prior to the mutation.

Neofunctionalization is the acquisition of a novel bioactive mechanism, such as an affinity for a receptor that activates or inhibits a physiological function or even a loss of bioactivity that accompanies or complements the functional variation novel to a toxin. It differs from loss of function not because certain functions are not absent, but because novel combinations of variables resulted in a toxin with bioactive effects distinct from the venom protein it was derived from, such as the domain losses from PIII metalloproteases, leading to the expression of PI and PII metalloproteases in some viper species (Brust et al., 2013). Taxon specificity refers to substantial variability in venom potency, sometimes sufficient to make one taxonomic group unaffected at biologically relevant levels compared to another taxa, which may be lethally affected at relevant or even lower than typically observed lethal doses for the given venom. The neofunctionalization of a taxon-specific mechanism of action, such as a ligand-binding toxin's affinity for a region conserved through many levels of taxonomic diversity being lost through a mutation that simultaneously allows it to bind and impact a similar or even the same ligand at a less conserved region may sound improbable but has been observed more than once. The affinity for the typical binding region of both spider and anemone sodium channel inhibitors was lost relative to the prototypical target of the toxin, a highly conserved region with a nearly universal sequence in the insect and shrimp ligand binding domains that, when bound, inhibited sodium channel. Both were originally evaluated as a loss of function due to the lack of a model organisms that expressed the sequence at the binding domain for which the toxin now had a greater affinity. As a result, neither showed loss of life or evidence of paralytic toxicity. Even binding affinities using specifically isolated receptors with the typical binding domain demonstrated the predicted drop in affinity. However, when the toxin was tested on a major pest species, one which expressed the second ligand-binding domain sequence which was susceptible to the mutated toxin, the rapidly induced lethal paralysis was assumed to be limited specifically to that species and was rapidly investigated, at significant cost, as a potential insecticide. Though they would have preferred it eradicate the invasive pest while sparing endogenous wildlife, the specific ligand sequence susceptible was not relevant to how costly the species were to humans.

The same trend was observed in an anemone sodium channel inhibitor which lost broader efficacy towards fish but gained efficacy towards a particular predating species of shrimp (Bende et al., 2014;Herzig et al., 2016;Sachkova et al., 2019;Schendel et al., 2019). This example also elucidated the mechanism through which the toxin described earlier gained an affinity towards a less conserved binding region, which varied enough between different taxa that only specific organisms were deleteriously impacted following envenomation.

div.head: Venom Pharmaceuticals
div.p: A peptide, exenatide 4, found in the venom of the Gila Monster (Heloderma suspectum), is a great example of the similarity that venom peptides have to endogenous peptides and proteins that are physiological effectors. This toxin exemplifies the utility of a modification that is especially necessary for the efficacy of any protein within a venom: specific structural modifications that prolong its lifetime in prey tissues. This non-endogenous ligand activates a receptor whose endogenous ligand (glucagon) has been produced commercially for decades but which lacked utility due to the rapid rate at which it is broken down by endogenous catabolic mechanisms. The exact reason for the presence in the venom of a molecule that does not seem to pose any significant toxic threat is poorly understood. However, a commercially available form of this peptide that appears to be highly effective in many cases for type 2 diabetes is now currently available under the brand name Byetta. This peptide is similar enough to the crucial blood sugar-regulating peptide, human glucagon (GLP-1) to mimic its activity, but is different enough that it is not recognized and broken down by the bodies' natural enzymes; therefore, it has a half-life that is long enough to exert useful pharmacological effects after administration.

This drug may even promote satiety; as a result, it treats overeating, one of the underlying factors that lead to the development and progression of type 2 diabetes (Dungan & Buse, 2005). While not currently prescribed for its appetite-suppressant effects, the obesity epidemic is a worldwide health crisis, and any potential remedies are of obvious importance. Byetta is a powerful example of how an unlikely effect can be derived from an unlikely source of abundant bioactive proteins.
Therefore, careful screening of venom peptides can yield medical breakthroughs in areas not immediately related to the most obvious effects of envenomation.

Among biologics older than 10 years (Darrow et al., 2020), therapeutics that contain all or some of the natural protein that produced the desirable effect, nearly 10% were inspired by venom toxins, and the vast majority (over two thirds) were derived from components found in reptile venoms (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2018). The trend of naturally sourced, approved drugs derived from venom in the past 50 years is increasing. Since 2015, approximately 500% more biologics are approved annually relative to the two prior decades, but none of those in trials or approved come from non-front-fanged snake (NFFS) venoms (U.S.

Food and Drug Administration, 2018). One of the most impactful venom-derived drugs was commercialized by deriving a small, non-protein based, organic molecule that mimicked the residues of the ligand binding domain, and it led to one of the most adopted methods of blood pressure regulation was captopril, the first commercialized drug that worked through the mechanism of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition. The angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors regulate high blood pressure without the risks posed by osmotic disruption induced by diuretics, or by the dangers of hypotension by drugs directly reducing heart rate or stroke volume. As a result, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition has been pursued and adapted through three generations of pharmaceutical families, the most recent remaining among the most common methods of managing hypertension today (Camargo et al., 2012;Ferreira, 1965). The antiplatelet aggregation drug, sold first under the brand name Aggrastat, as well as the later arginine-glycine-aspartic domain-targeting disintegrin from Sistrurus venom, work through similar mechanisms to target a potential complicating factor leading to unwanted clots following surgical procedures (Lang et al., 2012;Scarborough et al., 1991).

Exenatide, discussed above, mimics the GLP-1 receptor's endogenous ligand while avoiding the efficacy-limiting speed of enzymatic breakdown that injection of the endogenous molecule experiences (Furman, 2012). However, the half-life was still far lower than would be desirable, leading to multiple patents all fulfilling the goal of incrementally increasing the halflife and avoiding rapid degradation. Further modifications included addition of lysine (requiring enzymatic activation) and, when mixed with unmodified exenatide, the two facilitate a reasonable approximation of spacing out two injections. Patents of this and a more recent method of extending duration of efficacy (a major advantage for a drug that cannot be taken orally) account for three of the eleven current reptile venom-derived pharmaceuticals (Wysham et al., 2017).

Bothrops asper (Fer-de-lance) and B. moojeni (Brazilian Lancehead) venoms both produce a thrombin-like serine protease, with consistency and specificity that make certain derived pharmaceuticals candidates for treating acute clot-related pathological emergencies, such as deep vein thrombosis. Long used in many parts of the world, the United States approved emergency and surgical anticoagulant use later than other parts of the world (He et al., 2007).

The use of these enzymes in other applications are still awaiting approval in the United States, while in certain countries they form part of the combination therapies of gels and synthetic coverings applied to damaged tissue to facilitate more rapid and more complete tissue growth in areas lacking the necessary tissue volume and shape for healing (Mazzucco et al., 2008).

Cobratide is an alpha neurotoxin applied to reduce severe pain and is in clinical trials in humans. Alongside novel methods of more accurately controlling and monitoring systemic loads of the drug, it appears effective at reducing nociception while avoiding doses that induce the respiratory depression associated with alpha neurotoxin envenomation (Chen et al., 2016;Gazerani & Cairns, 2014). The potential applications of methods allowing safe application of an alpha neurotoxin without the risk of accidentally inducing the voluntary muscle paralysis or respiratory depression would allow the conceivable applications of countless toxins whose current effective therapeutic doses are far too close to their toxic doses to consider direct applications. However, the discrimination of an alpha neurotoxin with an affinity for the analgesic receptors, but without the specificity for the mammalian receptors associated with motor control of respiration, would make the degree of monitoring required a far less significant requirement. Candidates for a less toxic analgesic with reduced paralytic efficacy would seem a potential reason to evaluate the diverse group of alpha neurotoxins recognized for their relative reduction in affinity for the receptors that induce mammalian toxicity. Yet the most abundant source of them remains largely untapped.

Proteins originally sourced or modified from a venom protein make up 15% of peptide drugs, one of the most rapidly growing subtypes of pharmaceuticals, as previously discussed in the research of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2022). As the technology that makes protein-based medications viable develops, so does recognition of their benefits. Their specificity and reliance on not only the binding domains of their ligands but on the presence, absence, or variability of adjacent regions making up the subtypes of the impacted receptors and even on the presence or absence of structures independent of that being affected, as evidenced by the efficacy of the protein modification implemented by Ma et al. (2020) and also by the specificity of the scorpion venom that inspired it. An adaptation that demonstrates how the relevance that reptile venoms were those derived to create 11 of the 16 biologics represents only a small portion of the potential utility that improving our understanding and expanding our databases of reptile venoms might benefit the development of novel protein pharmaceuticals (Oliveira et al., 2022). Among venomous reptiles, there are three distinct glands recognized, with consensus among experts, as venom glands and clearly defined types of reservoirs. Those of helodermatid lizards, a single genus with several species representing the lizards recognized (without debate) as venomous are limited not only by their minimal taxonomic variability but by their venoms tendency to remain highly conserved over time periods that snakes' venoms have shown far greater levels of diversification (Koludarov et al., 2014). Front-fanged venomous snakes, with rapidly delivered venoms, are likely the second most taxonomically diverse and are also the focus of the vast majority of reptile venom research. Tasoulis et al. (2022) estimated that 12% of elapids and ~25% of viper venoms had been researched well enough to be included in their review of compositional variation. This criterion required multiple comprehensive proteomic or transcriptomic analyses of each species included, revealing that every detected toxin in one-fifth of front-fanged species has been sequenced. While this is vastly different from stating that those proteins have all been evaluated for all potential utility, it is indicative of the degree to which we have neglected study of the third source of reptile venoms, rear-fanged venomous snakes.

Estimates vary, as we have not yet collected samples from most species of snakes that are likely to contain active Duvernoy's venom glands, but the five species Tasoulis et al. (2022) were able to include represent, at most, 0.7% of NFFS venom. Kardong (2002), and a separate estimate by Mackessy (2002), both estimated that ~700 species of colubriform snakes possessed Duvernoy's venom glands. Kardong emphasized that some proteins and toxins, which have potentially evolved and adapted for roles which other reptile venoms have not, may lead to variability within familiar toxin families in ways that will ultimately lead to broader understanding of some of those venoms' mechanisms of action. The logical focus of any search meant to uncover toxins with novel variability in mechanisms and bioactivities within well-studied toxin families (such as those found in front-fanged venomous snakes) should be the contents of the > 99% of Duvernoy's venom gland secretions that remain undescribed, despite recognition of consisting of the same toxin families as front-fanged venomous snake toxins that all prior research on reptile toxins is focused. Furthermore, as discussed previously (Junqueira- de-Azevedo et al., 2016), there is uncertainty in the workflows of the various venomic methods that can fail to represent the possibility that other toxins, bioactivities, and structural variabilities were present in the venoms.

div.head: Historical Focus of Snake Venom Research
div.p: Medically relevant snake envenomations are limited to species with the classic elapid (solenoglyph) or viperid (proteroglyphs) dentitions, with few exceptions. Their hollow, fixed or hinged, and enlarged front fangs allow rapid injection of venom into prey or assailant.

Concurrent with venom glands containing lumina filled with exocytosed venom, voluntary compression via skeletal muscle allows metered delivery in fractions of a second (Mackessy, 2022;Westeen et al., 2020). The NFFS venom species possess a delivery mechanism that typically prohibits the delivery of equivalent doses without much longer contact times. Rearfanged (opisthoglyphous) snakes have fangs facilitating capillary flow of venom through grooves as well as by mechanisms that do not require any specialized structures. Paired teeth positioned in close enough proximity will produce a single puncture wound, and the channel created by the two fangs and the two edges of the punctured epithelium effectively facilitate capillary flow of venom. Duvernoy's venom glands typically lack a lumen or other extracellular storage space typical of front-fanged snake venom glands.

Three genera of opisthoglyphous snakes are recognized as able to rapidly deliver potentially fatal doses of venom to humans: Rhabdophis tigrinum (Hifumi et al., 2022) Dispholidus typus (Pla, Petras, et al., 2017), and Thelotornis sp. The latter two species belong to the subfamily Colubrinae are the only opisthoglyphous species to cause fatalities with any regularity following bites (Modahl et al., 2020;Modahl, Mrinalini, & Mackessy, 2018).

Philodryas olfersii has also led to fatal envenomation, and other species within the Philodryas genus have caused multiple medically significant envenomation cases. Though life threatening symptoms would be exceptional, their bites have demonstrated far more deleterious effects in humans than most opisthoglyphous species (Urra et al., 2019). While not a public health hazard compared to other venomous snakes, Colubrinae, Dipsadinae, and Natricinae subfamilies contain species that have produced severe or lethal envenomations. Rhabdophis tigrinum belongs to a poorly studied subfamily Natricinae of eastern Asia (Guo et al., 2022). According to the review by Tasoulis et al. (2022), venomic research has provided the necessary data to describe which toxin families are present and, on average, how much each of those contribute to the overall compositions of one of five front-fanged species' venoms included.

Characterizations of novel colubrid venoms based on proteomic or transcriptomic methods sometimes include details of bioactivities that were never practically evaluated. Schramer et al. (2022) used a combination of proteomics and the biological analyses of toxicity, cytotoxicity, effect on clotting time and certain enzymatic activities to characterize a novel colubrid venom. Bioactivities of components that weren't assayed in isolation is justified by citing a characterization that did conduct analyses of isolated components because that species possesses a similar venotype (Modahl & Mackessy, 2019). Should any variability exist within the bioactivities of similar components they will likely be overlooked if the analyses that would reveal them are excluded.

div.head: Rear-Fanged Venom Composition and Novelties
div.p: Five years after their compositional review opted not to include NFFS venom due to lack Colubrinae with a reliance on taxon-specific three-finger toxin (3FTx) and the snake venom metalloproteinases (SVMP)-reliant Dipsadinae (Modahl, Frietz, & Mackessy., 2018;Peichoto et al., 2011). Several Colubrinae, while not lacking SVMPs, have a far greater abundance of 3FTx (Mackessy, 2022;Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009;Peichoto et al., 2012;Tasoulis et al., 2022). These phenotypes are not so consistent as to warrant conclusions about whether or not detailed characterizations will reveal components typically considered absent in the previously characterized venoms of a family as definitive of the dipsadine venotype as Philodryas. Even though P. agasazzi possesses the metalloprotease-dominated venotype expected, it is transcriptomic composition consists of 20% 3FTx, a rarity in dipsadine venoms that is consistent with expression of 3FTx in the proteomic composition of the venom, though it is produced in quantities that make up only about one tenth of what it contributes to the transcriptomic analysis as only 1.5-2% of the proteins expressed during collection of P. agasazzi venom are 3FTx (Tioyama et al., 2023). Another venom expressed by rear-fanged venomous snakes, which demonstrates effects that are dramatically apparent as a result of their potency towards humans, is addressed by Debono et al. (2017). The colubrine Dispholidus typus can produce procoagulants at quantities and bioactivities that have led to envenomation with sometimes fatal results accompanied by disseminated intravascular coagulopathy like symptoms as a result of extremely potent factor X-activating metalloproteases, demonstrating that while dipsadine and colubrine venotypes have properties which are consistent and commonly described by the trends forming a dichotomy. Though exceptions and variations to the bioactivities and identities of compositional elements occur without necessarily producing a loss or gain of sufficient bioactivities or abundances of most proteins that they would be observed through analyses using only whole venom samples. Furthermore, some of those already distinguished have been significant, and present even between venoms sampled from closely related species with consistent venotypes to illustrate examples of what misconceptions might be born through assumptions of Schramer et al. (2022).

Other toxins present in the non-front-fanged venomous snake (NFFVS) include phospholipase A2 (Huang & Mackessy, 2004), L-amino acid oxidases (Mackessy et al., 2020), and C-type lectins, either as monomeric toxins or, potentially, domains of SVMP P-IIId subtype toxins. The latter have been identified in Viperidae and Dipsadinae venoms (de Araújo & dos Santos, 1997;Modahl et al., 2020;Panagides et al., 2017;Peichoto et al., 2009;Peichoto et al., 2007), and this subtype of SVMP is associated with potent gelatinase activity. In addition, though those isolated from rear fanged species have not been equally evaluated, two viper SVMP P-IIId subtype complexes, defined by two C-type lectin monomers covalently bound in addition to the typical residues, are both described as inhibiting collagen-induced platelet aggregation (Leonardi et al., 2008); one was further tested and demonstrated activation of coagulation factor X (Takeya et al., 1992). This suggests that P-IIId metalloproteases in Dipsadinae venoms may cause additional coagulopathies compared to those with SVMPs showing no covalent involvement of C-type lectins. Two novel toxin families expressed by NFFS venom but not in front-fanged snake venoms, include matrix metalloproteases (multiple species, including several within the genus Rhabdophis (Komori et al., 2017), and veficolins, thought to induce or facilitate toxic coagulopathies based on the role of mammalian filocans (OmPraba et al., 2010). Though transcriptomally evident in other species, veficolins have definitively been found in expressed venom of Cerberus rynchops (OmPraba et al., 2010), a member of a relatively small family (Homalopsidae) distinct from the Colubrinae, Natricinae, or Dipsadinae.

One of the most abundant subtypes of toxin in many Colubrinae from New World and Old-World species, and not entirely lacking from some Dipsadinae currently evaluated, are nonconventional 3FTx. Non-conventional 3FTx are also present in elapid venoms, but they are typically distinct and do not share a common property of NFFS venom 3FTx: taxon specificity.

Dimeric non-conventional 3FTx with a lack of any mammalian toxicity are also unique to NFFS venom; though covalent dimers are relatively rare in both, they are expressed in considerably large proportion by Boiga irregularis (Pawlak et al., 2009) and, as described in this research, Trimorphodon lambda. Given the number of elapids whose greatest threat to humans is posed by the effects of non-selective 3FTx, the selectivity of this component may potentially even explain some of the apparent lack of envenomation symptoms in humans bitten by species like Boiga irregularis, despite their rapid induction of paralysis at doses of the dimeric neurotoxin, irditoxin, that rival the toxicity of alpha cobratoxin in chicks, Hemidactylus geckos, and Anolis.

Further research into the toxicity towards different squamate species performed in this thesis details some of the even greater level of taxon selectivity, especially in monomeric nonconventional 3FTx.

div.head: Aims
div.p: A more thorough characterization of two species, Philodryas baroni, a relatively understudied member of the dipsadine genus Philodryas, and the colubrine species
Trimorphodon lambda, will be the main topic of this chapter. As one Dipsadinae and one

Colubrinae were evaluated, we expect to see some degree of the dichotomy suggested by Tasoulis et al. (2022). In fact, prior studies have revealed both to be stereotypes of their relative venotypes. However, neither venom has been scrutinized for a wide array of bioactivities or scrutinized for variations in reduced vs unreduced banding patterns on sodium dodecyl-sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) outside of samples that appraised the whole venom at once. Thus, research proceeded with a focus on determining whether variabilities between both one another and their relatives are either similar to or lack apparent additional components. Some of the variations that are of greatest interest to those who are bioprospecting of such narrow focus that its potent minimum hemorrhagic dose has been recognized though the LD50 and overall toxicity remained conjecture (Sánchez et al., 2014). This research demonstrates that P. baroni venom is highly toxic, rivaling or exceeding the toxicity of most type 1, nonneurotoxic, pit viper venoms, and non-specific between mice and lizard models, while T. lambda venom incapacitates Hemidactylus frenatus at a similar dose that does not cause lethal effects until significantly higher doses while the neurotoxic effects are absent in mice, which tolerate doses twenty times greater than those of P. baroni venom.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Snake venoms are solutions containing a heterogenous mixture of ions, small organic molecules, proteins, and complexes including metalloproteases, glycosylated proteins, and both noncovalent and covalently bound multimeric protein complexes (Mackessy, 2021;Pawlak et al., 2009). The reviews of protein family variation by Tasoulis and Isbister (2017) and Tasoulis et al.

(2022) included only five species of non-front fanged venomous snakes (NFFVS), representative of only two of the three families of NFFVS responsible for fatal human envenomation. Reviews of those publications that have focused on analyses of NFFVS venoms mention their bioprospecting potential (Brandehoff et al., 2019;Kardong, 2002;Mackessy, 2002;Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009;Sánchez et al., 2014). Multiple reviews are centered specifically around rear-fanged snake venoms as an untapped resource despite their lower complexity and less diverse pool of bioactive proteins than those of front fanged species, primarily because they are global in distribution and are much more numerous than front-fanged species (Brandehoff et al., 2019;Fry et al., 2003;Junqueira-de-Azevedo et al., 2016;Mackessy, 2002Mackessy, , 2021;;Modahl & Mackessy, 2019). Most of the comprehensive analyses of a NFFVS venom are based on the combination of proteomics, transcriptomics, and genomics, collectively referred to as venomics.

As the most comprehensive and efficient method of discriminating protein families using homology to previously recognized toxins, venomics is a logical approach to evaluating the countless NFFVS venoms remaining completely undescribed. However, the lack of a detailed database of NFFVS venom proteins greatly hinders the effectiveness of an -omics approach.

Studies driven by observable effects and distinct bioactivities of both whole venoms or isolated toxins dominated the focus of venom research prior to -omics technologies. One potential issue with relying on venomics alone is that venoms/toxins are described based on a combination of transcript base and amino acid sequences, often excluding evaluations of lethality, cytotoxicity, neurotoxicity, or enzymatic activities. Typically, the more homologous a new toxin is to a toxin previously included in a database, the less likely that it will be evaluated for variation in bioactivity. Perhaps a lack of research driven by first observing bioactive impacts and activities, instead of just sequence homology and variability, is one reason why this large diversity of reptile venoms (i.e., NFFVS venoms), a reservoir of natural toxins with commercial potential, has never produced a single therapeutic drug candidate.

The NFFVS make up an estimated 50% of the diversity of species of colubriform snakes (Mackessy, 2002). Though they likely rival the species diversity of viperids and elapids combined, the exact number remains unknown due to lack of sufficient research on their venoms.

However, even highly conservative estimates would define the range of species with accurate compositional analyses of their venoms at < 3% of > 150 species (Tasoulis & Isbister, 2017;Tasoulis et al., 2022). Even among those species whose venoms have been studied, none are the source of patented compounds or are being subjected to more than the most preliminary evaluations of therapeutic, biologic, and biomimetic potential.

The research presented here focused on contrasting P. baroni and T. lambda venoms using practical methods to discriminate, evaluate, and isolate components of interest prior to sequencing them. Components of interest, if able to be purified and bioactive, were sequenced and compared to transcriptomic and proteomic databases both to confirm suspected toxin family and to determine whether previous venomic studies of closely related species reveal similar compounds. After identifying and isolating toxins, bioactivities, cytotoxicity, and specific toxicity towards mammals, lizards, or birds were evaluated. The venoms of two rear-fanged snakes lacking detailed transcriptomic or proteomic compositional analyses, but that are both members of the same genus as one of the only other comparative analyses of a South American Dipsadinae and North American Colubrinae, are Philodryas patagoniensis and Trimorphodon biscutatus (Peichoto et al., 2012). Both venoms have demonstrably variable bioactivities relative to those of the previously evaluated species. P. baroni venom, for instance, contains no threefinger toxins (3FTx) or evidence of enzymatic components besides metalloproteases, an activity also observed in T. lambda venom, yet it is potency towards Hemidactylus is five-fold greater, and is equally toxic to Non-Swiss Albino mice, making it over 25 times more potent than the highly taxon-specific T. lambda venom. Their venom's relative bioactivities are consistent with what would be expected based on a dichotomy described by Tasoulis et al. (2022), suggesting a reliance on snake venom metalloproteases or 3FTx, respectively. The compositional domination of the P. baroni proteome by snake venom metalloproteinases (SVMP) is more obvious than the dominance of 3FTx in T. lambda venom through size exclusion (SE), sodium dodecyl-sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), and enzymatic assays. T. lambda, however, does cause taxon-specific flaccid paralysis with a relatively large effective index, similar to other neurotoxic Colubrinae (Mackessy et al., 2020;Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009). Even analyses of crude venom and bioactive components of these two species' venoms provide evidence that NFFVS are good bioprospecting reservoirs that may contain potent, rare, or novel combinations of bioactive proteins.

The range of protein variation within a species' venom can be extreme, even within a species found within the same general regions. Front-fanged snake venom composition varies at all taxonomic levels, including between and within species (inter-versus intra-specific variation)

sometimes corresponding to population variation (Saviola et al., 2016). The venoms of vipers in the genus Crotalus include species without neurotoxic venoms and diverse collections of multiple variations of multiple toxin families, as well as the species with the least diverse, yet most toxic, venom towards multiple taxa of model organisms. Crotalus tigris has a venom with a greater dependance on a single toxin (that is also expressed in other species within the genus as well as with highly homologous variations throughout no less than half a dozen species), and it is very potent (Margres et al., 2021). Consider how misleading our study of pitviper, especially

Crotalus, venoms would be if this were the single highly studied venom, ostensibly representing dozens of species and multiple genera. As another example of variation, individuals of an Australian elapid species of the same population express different protein families in their venoms (Tasoulis et al., 2022). Tasoulis and Isbister (2017) specifically elaborated on the tendency of compositional venomic studies to use only a single individual to describe the venom of a species. Many recent reviews thoroughly examine the effectiveness of modern venomic methods (e.g., Tan, 2022;Tasoulis et al., 2022) at identifying which family of toxin protein they express as well as determining the most homologous proteins from prior studies. The major shortcoming of basing assumed bioactivities of components on the closest match is when, like Schramer et al. (2022), only a single publication contains a species from the same family and region with the bioactivities and variations also based on a hybrid transcriptomic methodology.

The logical outcome of such methods suggests that venomic methods are excellent for rapidly discriminating similar toxins and major compositional variations. However, only five species, representing < 1% of NFFVS, can compete with the ~20% of viper and elapid species' venomes detailed sufficiently to be included in a protein complexity study (Tasoulis et al., 2022) a number which did not increase over the 5 years separating these two reviews.

Metalloproteases are present in a majority of colubriform snake venoms (Mackessy, 2010a), and P. baroni and T. biscutatus lambda (during an evaluation prior to elevation to species) were no exceptions. T. b lambda was determined to express monomeric alpha 3FTx in the same reviews and studies (Sánchez et al., 2014;Saviola et al., 2014). Sánchez et al. (2014) described potent hemorrhagic effects induced in mice at low microgram doses of P. baroni venom. However, the LD50 was not evaluated due to material limitations, as was the case for T. lambda venom during trimorphin isolation (Huang & Mackessy, 2004). Based on the potent hemorrhagic activity in mice by P. baroni and the tendency to express avian-and squamatespecific 3FTx in many colubrine venoms, the overall toxicity, as well as the expectation that lizards will be impacted at much lower doses than mice, could both be expected to depend on the relative levels of metalloprotease activity in their venoms. This trend of more toxic type 1 venoms is very distinct from the trend observed in front-fanged venomous snake toxicity towards mammals, including humans, where those venoms with presynaptic neurotoxins, in the case of some vipers, or alpha-neurotoxic 3FTx, as in many elapids, nearly always show LD50s far lower than those of the venoms with the highest metalloprotease activities but no neurotoxic components (Doley et al., 2008). Pla, Sanz, et al. (2017) suggested that the driving factor behind the coagulopathies following Boomslang envenomation are metalloproteases instead of the serine proteases long suspected to be responsible, which may describe why they pose a higher threat towards mammals as large as humans but are not as distinctly responsible for the "tenderizer" effect observed when comparing the "tenderizer and/or tranquilizer" spectra seen in crotaline venoms (Mackessy, 2010b, p. 8).

Due to the paucity of opistoglyphous venoms that have been deconstructed through protein purification via SE chromatography, reduced SDS-PAGE versus unreduced SDS-PAGE, and other techniques, we may be over-reliant on assumptions that trends observed in the elapid and viper venoms that we have deconstructed in this way can be as easily interpreted through proteomic sequences and homologies seen in NFFSV proteins. As venoms that we are only just beginning to understand, and still speculating on the ecological roles of, it seems presumptive to assume that we can be as confident about assumptions about composition and activity that have not been practically evaluated as we can about those front-fanged snake venoms with extensive databases that also contain evaluated venom toxins, in addition to simple catalogs of proteomes or transcriptomes. By establishing the variability in enzymatic activities, potencies, and quaternary structure of individual toxin proteins in individuals, species, genera, and families, one can create a more accurate database of colubriform venom proteins to compare against the far more rapid, but often less reliant on practical bioactivity evaluation, venomic techniques.

Accurately interpreting where deviations from the typical composition and bioactive profiles exist are directly associated with the potential that we will notice applications for biologics, and protein traits that could potentially be applied to synthesis of novel peptide drugs.

div.head: A1
div.p: Determine enzymatic bioactivities of venoms and responsible compositional elements.

div.head: A2
div.p: Determine the relative toxicities (mouse versus Anolis) as well as notable presence or absence of observable variations in toxic mechanisms.

div.head: A3
div.p: Evaluate wild-caught Trimorphodon lambda individuals for major variation in venom composition.

div.head: Venom Extraction
div.p: Colubrid venom was manually extracted through the protocol outlined in Hill and Mackessy (1997). T. lambda was wild-caught at various locations within their range in Arizona. depending on species and prior reaction); the muscarinic parasympathetic nervous system parasympathetic nervous system stimulant pilocarpine-HCl (6 mg/kg) was administered following immobilization. Due to the dehydrating effects of pilocarpine, rear-fanged snakes were soaked in a secure container with water up to a depth ~3/4 that of the individual's diameter for 12-24 hr prior to extraction; snakes in stages of ecdysis were not extracted. A minimum time between extractions of an individual was two months, though typically 3 to 6 months were allowed. Venom was centrifuged at 9,500 x g, frozen and lyophilized and stored at a minimum of -20 o C.

div.head: Size Exclusion Chromatography
div.p: Venom was collected from multiple extractions until 40-100 mg of lyophilized venom was accumulated. The aggregated material was then solubilized in SE buffer (25 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, 5 mM CaCl2 pH 6.8), for a total of 1-1.5 mL. Samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 9,500 x g before using a syringe tip filter (0.45 µm), avoiding any pelleted solid or distinct layers of congealed mucous or otherwise non-aqueous layers. The solubilized and filtered venom was gravity loaded onto a BioGel P-100 (medium) SE column (2.6 x 89 cm). The SE chromatography was performed at 4 °C over several days at a constant flow rate of approximately 6.0 mL/hr, collecting fractions of ~3 mL every 30 min. These fractions were labeled by order of elution and their protein content evaluated by reading the absorbance at 280 nm. Based on the chromatograph obtained when plotting fractions versus absorbance, the distinct elution peaks were assayed for specific activities, run on SDS-PAGE gels to estimate size and number of proteins present, and the individual partially purified venom components were combined. Dialysis tubing used (spell out) molecular weight (MW) cut-offs of approximately one-half the lowest observed SDS-PAGE band's MW, with two consecutive changes of two liters of Millipore-filtered water for at least 12 hr each or against 20 mM ammonium acetate (to minimize formation of precipitates).

div.head: Fast Performance Liquid Chromatography: Anion and Cation Exchange Cation Exchange
div.p: Using Unicorn software and either a 5 mL SP Hi-Trap or a 1 mL CM cation exchange column, lyophilized venom or partially purified venom component was dissolved in 250 µL of 20 mM MES buffer pH 6.2 (buffer A). After centrifuging and filtering through a 0.45 µm syringe filter, the sample was fractionated via fast performance liquid chromatography. After 10 mL (or at least two full column volumes) of buffer A washed unbound material from the column (at 1 mL/min flow rate), a 50 min (50 fraction) 0.5 ml/min flow rate began with a simple gradient of 0-50% buffer B (A+1M NaCl). Protein peaks were recorded at 280 nm.

div.head: Anion Exchange
div.p: The same methods were employed during anion exchange as cation exchange with the substitution of a 1 mL or 5 mL DEAE column as indicated. The samples were dissolved in buffer A containing 25 mM HEPES at pH 8.0. Any variation in gradient is indicated on individual figures and will either indicate a 0-30% rather than 0-50% gradient or a gradient running to 25%
B and then rapidly climbing to either 50% or 100% B over 10 min, a 5-min plateau, and returning over 1 min to 0% B. These variations are either indicated on figures or in their titles.

Fractions from each ion exchange method were combined based on chromatograms, as well as isolating the material that eluted prior to the start of the gradient "Breakthrough;" all those eluting after are denoted as a "Retained" peak.

div.head: Crude Venom Composition
div.p: Two hundred µg of crude venoms or SE peaks from individual or pooled samples of T. lambda and pooled P. baroni venom were run on HPLC using a Phenomenex Jupiter C18 250 x 4.6 mm, 5 µm, 300 Å pore column at < 1500 PSI. A 1 ml/min flow rate was maintained throughout the run. A gradient of 95% solution A (0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in Millipore-filtered water) to 100% solution B (0.1% TFA in 80% acetonitrile) was used (referred to hereafter as "colubrid venomics" method). The gradient ran for 120 min: 95% A from 0 to 5 min, 5-25% B until minute 15, 25-75% B until minute 100, increasing to 100% B over 5 min, maintaining 100% for 5 min, returning to 95% A over 2 min and then running without change for the remainder of the run (8 min).

div.head: Individual Venom Variation
div.p: The P. baroni venom yields were very low (approx. 5-10 mg of 25% protein as evaluated at 280nm) and compared via SDS-PAGE. T. lambda yields were large (approximately 20-40 mg of 50% protein as evaluated at 280nm) and both specimens were independently evaluated through SE, reverse phase, enzyme activity, and additional samples. Five wild-caught T. lambda venoms were analyzed using reverse phase high performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC) crude venomics methodology.

div.head: Detection of Multimeric Toxins
div.p: Contrasting reduced and unreduced samples of SE-purified fractions on SDS-PAGE led to recognition of bands formed only after reduction. Comparing reduced and unreduced samples on MALDI-TOF MS was used to confirm the masses to a higher degree of certainty than possible with SDS-PAGE.

div.head: Lambditoxin: Isolation and Identification of an Unknown Dimeric Trimorphodon Lambda Toxin
div.p: The RP-HPLC Colubrid Venomics method, using a 40-min gradient from 30% to 50% B, allowed discrimination and collection of the two peaks eluting from the second SE peak of T.
lambda, where SDS-PAGE revealed absence of a higher mass band, in addition to the presence of a roughly one-half mass band, under non-reducing conditions relative to reducing conditions.

Samples were prepared for Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization Time of Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) as described below. A sample of the isolated protein was also sent to Dr. Anthony Saviola at Scripps University, California, for liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) proteomic sequencing.

div.head: C-Type Lectin Isolation from Philodryas Baroni Venom
div.p: Analysis of SE-fractions across the bifurcated first peaks, using SDS-PAGE under reducing and non-reducing conditions, revealed the presence of lower mass bands only after reduction. These proteins were isolated by a combination of SE and ion exchange chromatography.

div.head: Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption Ionization Time of Flight Mass Spectrometry
div.p: The matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) evaluations of purified proteins or dimers included samples that were either reduced or unreduced. Both intact and reduced sample were dissolved at ~1mg/mL in 50% acetonitrile + 0.1% trifluoracetic acid (TFA), and 2 µL was mixed with an identical quantity of sinapinic acid matrix (10 mg/mL in identical solution) and then spotted onto target plates for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Reduced samples went through an incubation protocol as described by Modahl and Mackessy (2016), prepared by incubating with dithiothreitol (DTT)

and covalently modifying the unbound cysteines with iodoacetamide. Samples of purified toxin were dissolved at ~1 mg/mL protein concentration (based on Nanopore absorbance at 280 nm) in 50% acetonitrile + 0.1% TFA and combined with sinapinic acid matrix (5 mg/mL final concentration after mixing with samples just prior to spotting on plates). The MALDI-TOF-MS was performed on a Bruker Ultraflex MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometer in the Metabolomics Facility at Colorado State University (Fort Collins, Colorado).

div.head: Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry Sequencing
div.p: Purified samples of proteins requiring sequence data were sent to Dr. Anthony Saviola at Scripps Institute for LC-MS/MS proteomic sequencing. In each of the samples where confirmation is supported by LC-MS/MS methods, the sequence coverage was ~50% for lambditoxin and over 80% for both C-type lectin evaluations, as well as having over 1,000 spectral counts, with those being at least twice as high as the next highest spectral counts for any protein not of the same type.

div.head: Sodium Dodecyl Sulphate Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis
div.p: Crude venoms of P. baroni and T. lambda as well as SE purified peaks were evaluated with SDS-PAGE under reducing and non-reducing conditions on the same gel if possible and on separate gels if the number of samples to evaluate exceeded the number of wells.

The SDS-PAGE was conducted on NuPAGE bis-tris 12% acrylamide mini gels based on both the protocol accompanying the product and the methodology described in Smith and Mackessy (2016). All SDS-PAGE runs underwent identical running, staining, and imaging procedures. A constant 175-voltage was applied for 45 min (approximately 125 mA initially).

Gels were stained with 0.1%. Coomassie brilliant blue R-250 in 50% methanol and 20% acetic acid (v/v) overnight with gentle shaking and destained in 30% methanol, 7% glacial acetic acid in dd H2O (v/v) for 2-4 hr prior to being placed in a storage solution (7% acetic acid, v/v). When reduced samples were loaded onto gels with unreduced samples, the DTT reduction was replaced by use of 5% -mercaptoethanol incubation at 10 minutes and 95 °C. Gels were imaged using an Epson scanner.

div.head: Enzyme Activities
div.p: Crude venoms, SE purified peaks, or ion exchange chromatography peaks were evaluated for the presence of various enzymatic activities based on the established protocols (Smith & Mackessy, 2016).

div.head: Metalloprotease Activity Towards Azocasein
div.p: Using azocasein substrate (Aird & da Silva, 1991), at 500 uL of 2 mg/mL azocasein in 50 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl pH 8.0 buffer, into which the crude venom, SE peak, or other isolation product, was dissolved at a starting quantity (if known) of 20 µg of crude venom in the same buffer, if possible, though SE buffer or aqueous suspension of 50uL or less was sometimes used. One mg of azocasein in 500 uL of buffer was added as substrate to each tube including triplicates of control tubes containing only buffer, substrate, and the same carrier as samples and otherwise treated identically to samples. Substrate was added while samples were on ice to minimize variation in reaction duration as samples were prepared. Incubation was at 37 °C for 15, 30, or 60 min depending on the approximate expected level of activity, aiming to stop the assay at a point when the relationship between change in absorbance and rate of substrate production have a linear relationship. Following incubation all tubes are placed on ice and reactions are stopped with 250 μL of 0.5 M trichloroacetic acid and vortexing and then allowed to warm. Once at room temperature, all tubes are centrifuged on a Joun 50 cm diameter centrifuge for 10 min at 2000 rpm until precipitate is compacted into a pellet and supernatant appears free of precipitate. Supernatant absorbance is read at 342 nm and specific activity is reported as Δ342nm/min/mg of venom protein (Smith & Mackessy, 2016).

div.head: L-Amino Acid Oxidase Activity
div.p: L-amino acid oxidase (LAAO) activity was measured by the assay outlined by Weissbach et al. (1960) as modified by Smith and Mackessy (2016). Controls and crude venom or SE peaks were run against controls with the same carrier but no venom proteins in 50 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, pH 8.0 buffer. Substrate was L-kynurenine solubilized in the same buffer at 1.04 mg/mL. 75 microliters of substrate were added to the venom-buffer mixture on ice (20 µg in 645 microliters for crude venoms, adjusted as necessary depending on purification and enzyme activity). Incubation lasted 60 min at 37 °C before termination with 750 microliters of 10% trichloroacetic acid. Absorbance was read, after samples had warmed to ~room temperature, at 331 nm by spectrophotometer. Activity was reported as change in absorbance per minute per mg venom protein.

div.head: Thrombin-Like Serine Protease Assays and Kallikrein-Like Serine Protease
div.p: Assays were both performed based on Smith and Mackessy (2016) adaptations of Mackessy (1993) protocols. Crude venom or SE peak material were solubilized in 50 mM HEPES, 100 mM NaCl, pH 8.0 at ~ 1-4 µg venom mass (even at higher than normal quantities, no activity was seen for either P. baroni or T. lambda) and 50 uL of BzPheValArg-pNA (Sigma Aldrich) substrate was added for thrombin-like activity while the substrate of Bz-ProPheArg-pNA (Bachem) acted as the substrate for kallikrein-like activity. Both were added to tubes already warmed to 37 °C, vortexed, and incubated for the indicated time (increased incubation time was a way to detect extremely low activity, if any, was present). Reactions for both were stopped with 50% acetic acid. Tubes were read at 405 nm and triplicate control values were subtracted from sample absorbances to obtain activities.

div.head: Phospholipase A2 Activity
div.p: Fifty μL of BioGel SE chromatography fractions were combined with 500 μL buffer, 10 μl of 4 mg/mL crude venom; purified and lyophilized components were combined with 540 μL buffer (10 mM tris-HCl, pH 8.0 with 10 mM CaCl2, 100 mM NaCl). Following addition of 50 μL of substrate to all experimental tubes and control tubes (triplicate) containing ddH2O in place of sample volume (Holzer & Mackessy, 1996), incubation at 37 °C and stopped with 50 μL of 2.5% Triton X-100. Results are either reported as 425 nm absorbance for pre-dialysis SE fractions or as absorbance value/min/mg protein (specific enzyme activity). Results reported in enzyme activity assays were always produced by replicate sample tubes.

Enzymatic activity of a SE or ion exchange fraction will typically not be reported as more than an absorbance value. These are presented to describe which fractions enzymatic proteins are eluting in or to compare the relative enzymatic activity of the proteins eluting in different portions of the same chromatography run.

div.head: Lethality Assays
div.p: The three Non-Swiss Albino lab mice or Hemidactylus frenatus lizards were treated with 5 μg/g doses of P. baroni or T. lambda venom. Depending on whether the majority of animals were alive, dead, or showed severe symptoms of any obvious type (loss of righting response was used as an indicator of muscular paralysis in lizards and mice), additional dose levels were established. Toxin concentration was evaluated with protein determination assays, either bicincionic acid (BCA) or nanodrop at 280nm. Venom stock was diluted with 0.9% saline to 50 µL bolus for lizards and weanling mice under 20 grams. 100 µL boluses were used for doses >25 µg/g and larger mice. Animals were evaluated for live/dead/paralysis symptoms at 24 hr. Doses were lowered by one-half if no animals survived, or doubled if a majority survived.

div.head: Philodryas Baroni Composition
div.p: BioGel P-100 SE results showed a single major bifurcated peak and a large downstream P. baroni venom demonstrated non-selective, highly toxic, and high metalloprotease activity, demonstrating composition including both a more typical P-III metalloprotease and a P-III metalloprotease that contained a C-type lectin, confirmed using LC/MS-MS. The highest spectral counts were seen for both the alpha and beta subunits (81% and 82% sequence coverage, respectively) of the C-type lectins from Philodryas olfersii (see Table 2.1). Note. AU = abslorbance units, SE = size exclusion, LAAO = L-amino acid oxidase. Activity of enzymes within typical P. baroni and T. lambda venoms activity, and the variations between the activities of the three enzymes detectable using the assays described in the methods reported using duplicate samples, triplicate controls, and reported in change in absorbance/mg protein (discerned via Nanodrop 280 nm)/minute (quantities and incubation times used produced final absorbances that did not exceed 1 AU for the same reason that the higher concentration sample used in Reynolds et. al was not used. Where no value is reported the sample fractions produced absorbances overlapping those produced by substrate incubated with buffer only. These were considered inactive. Enzyme assays from Smith and Mackessy (2016).

The presence of a banding pattern which was not observed prior to SE was faint but observable following SE chromatography. This banding became very pronounced following cation exchange of those size SE, where not only could two bands present under reducing conditions only (bands with masses of ~10 and ~12 kD), but also the higher mass band that is absent prior to reduction (also the absence of a band present at ~40-50 kD.

Following cation exchange of material isolated from the ascending portion of the bifurcated first peak, labeled 1, and the descending portion of the bifurcated peak, labeled peak 2, there were apparent compositional differences observable with SDS-PAGE (see Figure 2.1).
This difference was further confirmed with LC-MS/MS, with highest homology and the largest number of hits indicating a C-type lectin.
The P. baroni venom was negative for all enzyme assays, with the exception of metalloprotease activity as shown in Table 2.1.

div.head: Trimorphodon Lambda Venom Composition
div.p: The SDS-PAGE under reducing and non-reducing conditions of the SE peaks showed variation in a component of peak 2, with a decrease in size under reducing conditions (see Figure 2.5). The venom collected from one T. lambda individual demonstrated an almost complete absence of phospholipase activity. Under RP-HPLC and further analysis it was determined that three extractions over more than a 1-year period were used to obtain the venom collected for SE, and trimorphin was absent from all samples. This variation was not observed in the other live individual being extracted throughout the study, whose venom was identical in terms of presence of major peaks in three previously collected T. lambda venom samples examined with the Colubrid Venomics RP-HPLC analysis method. Therefore, the venom collected from this trimorphin-lacking individual is labeled as atypical, while those obtained from other individuals is noted as typical, or simply as T. lambda venom or venom components. While all lizards showed signs of flaccid paralysis at half the lethal dose, even the doses high enough to kill two of three mice did not produce any loss of righting or obvious signs of flaccid paralysis in surviving subjects or prior to death when lethal.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Bioprospecting proteins relies on following a set of assumptions made about the source of proteins, particularly where it is plausible that one might discover a novel lead with illuminating variations or potentially useful novel characteristics. Venoms provide a plethora of examples meeting desirable characteristics, including peptides that are stable and have high specificity for particular targets (Ma et al., 2020). However, that same set of assumptions means there are not bioprospecting efforts that target venoms reported to contain no components or bioactivities suggesting novel traits of the proteins present. Ma et al. (2020) remarks that venoms are such useful sources of inspiration because there are variants to relatively conserved families of proteins that have, over thousands to millions of years of adaptive evolution, produced bioactive proteins ideally grouped to determine potential mechanisms of specificity. Many peptide-based drug candidates are approached based on identifying the smallest functional amino acid sequences (through trial and error) and configuring them as building blocks that can generate products with predictable and desired bioactivities based on relative affinities and selectivity of the compositional elements. However, the structures and therefore functions of peptides and proteins are not exclusively determined by their primary sequences. Thus, natural proteins and their inherent mechanisms remain essential to research that may allow us to anticipate effects of, and benefit from bioactivities observed in, proteins large enough to be impacted by secondary, tertiary, and quaternary variations. In the particular modification to a biologic candidate described by Ma et al., mimicking the sequence of the observed binding site of a toxin was not nearly as valuable as observing the impact resulting from two independent binding sites interacting with two different ligands. An effect that was produced by peptidoglycan residues on the toxin was mimicked by dimerizing two smaller peptides in the biosynthetic molecule. This variation enabled the synthetic protein to demonstrate relative affinities for the desired therapeutic target several orders of magnitude greater than it previously displayed for the desired receptor.

The species chosen for the present research were similar to previously studied species, and the genera Philodryas and Trimorphodon are two of the few rear-fanged venoms with components that have been evaluated explicitly for potentially therapeutic efficacies.
Trimorphin, a PLA2 with potential anti-parasitic activity towards Leishmania, was identified in T.

lambda venom and comparatively evaluated against venoms of other rear-fanged species, including Philodryas venoms (Peichoto et al., 2011). More recently, Philodryas patagoniensis venom components were evaluated in a foot pad nociception and edema model similar to that used to evaluate peptides and small molecules for antinociceptive effects, though the results of this study were to conclude that metalloprotease activity was responsible for the edema induced, but that nociceptive effects were dependent on a different venom component (Lopes et al., 2017).

Based on the results of this research, the anti-leishmanial activity of T. lambda venom becomes more interesting when juxtaposed against the relative inefficacy of the venom (and especially the SE peak containing trimorphin) to induce cytotoxic effects until doses of an order of magnitude higher than P. baroni venom, and not evident at all in the second SE peak treatments. The presence of metalloproteases with variable potency, composition, integration of C-type lectin components, and potentially even covalent dimerism of P-III metalloproteases, though the last was not confirmed. One metalloprotease, patagonfibrase, was isolated from P.

patagoniensis, but this required multiple steps due to autodegradation, and N-terminal blockage prevented full sequencing of the protein. Patagonfibrase has been recognized as a hemorrhagic metalloprotease, demonstrating alpha-fibrinogen degradation as well as an inflammatory response (Peichoto et al., 2011;Peichoto et al., 2007). Whether or not P. patagoniensis contains as much variability between individual metalloproteolytic toxins as observed in P. baroni is not known, and therefore it is speculation whether patagonfibrase is the most significant toxin in this venom, leading to recognition of Philodryas sp. as clinically significant threats following human envenomations (Urra et al., 2019). Similarly, it may or may not be representative of the subtype of toxin that contributes most to the edema and nociceptive effects that are being evaluated for potential utility in identifying mechanisms of damage and potentially novel targets for therapeutics that could inhibit them (Lopes et al., 2017). A follow-up study using fractions of P.

baroni venom that contain only one of the two metalloproteases, containing C-type lectins and those that elute earlier, could focus on comparing not only the overall metalloprotease activity published here, but the extent of edema, hemorrhagic, and nociceptive effects, and individual

LD50s. This may allow a better appraisal of the potential potencies and clinical significance of opisthoglyphous species with similar venom phenotypes but without the same variability in metalloprotease composition.

Surprisingly, the metalloprotease activity of P. baroni venom prior to isolation of constituent components rivals many of those crotalids and other vipers that deliver classic "tenderizer" type venom. disintegrins are a major area of study for their potential applications towards a variety of medical applications (Rivas-Mercado & Garza-Ocañas, 2017), including the inhibition of metastases as suggested in Saviola et al. (2016) by tzabcanin, a venom component that has demonstrated impacts on adhesion in the melanoma cell line A375, a cancer line that is recognized to undergo decreased e-cadherin expression while increasing dependence on ncadherin. Demonstrated to disrupt junctions through impacts on the cellular V3 integrin, tzabcanin and some metalloproteases are a focus of many studies evaluating potential antimetastatic utility as well as identifying the rolls of various mechanisms in wound healing clotting and other aggregations of cells through carefully regulated adhesion conditions. This, and other processes impacted by snake venom metalloproteases, are integral to growth, wound healing and stem cell behavior, but also can facilitate fibrosis and cancer metastases. Thus, better recognition of the degree to which metalloproteases can vary in both potency and specificity could prove beneficial to understanding how we might modulate these effects as desired (Lamouille et al., 2014). This study helps provide recognition of examples where extreme variations in potency exist between proteins that are so similar have allowed the oversight of this variability, such as among venoms of Philodryas species.

The variations observed between similar species, such as P. baroni and P. patagoniensis, and conspecific individuals, such as the T. lambda specimens with and without PLA2, demonstrates that mistakes might be made by assuming that a single individual's venom is representative of their species or that a single species venom type is representative of their closest genetic and geographic relations. Therefore, it should be considered essential that multiple individuals be sampled before considering the results of venom analyses to be representative of a greater population. Limited sampling is often a tempting proposition due to the relative difficulty and more labor-intensive extractions typically required to obtain and aggregate similar quantities of opisthoglyphous snake venom compared to elapids or vipers of comparable size. Additionally, T. lambda venom typically contained about 75% of the expected protein mass, while only a quarter of the dried mass of P. baroni venom was proteinaceous. The P. baroni had a significantly lower venom volume yield than T. lambda, representative of an inconsistent relationship between opistoglyphous snake mass and quantity of venom yields. This abundance of toxin mass may explain how T. lambda venom plays a comparable ecological role in subduing susceptible prey without the potency observed in P. baroni venom. However, ecological factors driving prey evolution are both complicated, many, and highly debated among experts.

The T. lambda venom is secreted throughout the duration of a bite rather than delivered as an immediate bolus. Though a relatively small species, no larger than P. baroni, T. lambda express quantities of venom that rival those collected from far larger rear-fanged snake species.

With prolonged contact during a bite, it is not surprising that symptoms following human envenomation have occurred (Foley, 2002), though without paralysis or respiratory distress associated with disruption of the neuromuscular junction. During characterization, a dimeric 3FTx was described that can be readily isolated in bioactive conformations from crude venom using reverse phase HPLC. This makes the dimeric alpha neurotoxin, or lambditoxin, one of the most easily isolated and aggregated toxins among opisthoglyphous venoms. It is also a distinct toxin, sourced from a geographically distinct species, relative to either of the well-studied opisthoglyphous alpha neurotoxins, the heterodimeric irditoxin and monomeric denmotoxin from Boiga irregularis and Boiga dendrophila respectively. As a recognizably paralytic venom with at least a two-fold difference between paralytic and lethal doses in Hemidactylus frenatus, it is worth further study solely due to the desirability and therapeutic potential of reversible paralytics and the results of a comparative study observing the effects on chick biventer cervicis preps and neurotoxic opisthoglyphous snake venoms could be informative. A study revealed that only the venom of Trimorphodon biscutatus (the species to which T. lambda was considered a subspecies of at the time) showed increased muscle twitch strength following addition of a cholinergic agonist, and relative to the venoms of nearly one dozen Boiga species and various other opisthoglyphous colubrids, it required over three times the duration at a significantly higher dose to reduce twitch strength by fifty percent (Lumsden et al., 2004). Perhaps this component is responsible for the uniquely reversible paralysis observed only in chick biventer cervicis muscle preps.

Aside from the variation, or lack thereof, in venom composition that might be revealed by a more thorough proteomic evaluation of P. baroni and Philodryas patagoniensis, follow-up research comparing the tertiary and quaternary structures and confirmation of the subtypes suspected in P. baroni venom (presence/absence of C-type lectins) would be illuminating as Philodryas sp. are described expressing both SVMP P-III and snake venom matrix metalloproteases, but not metalloproteases in heterodimeric complexes with C-type lectins. In Trimorphodon, the influence of the enzymatic venom components may have been the reason that extremely high doses were lethal to mice, though it should be noted that at a dose of 50 ug/g in 10 g weanling mice, only two of the three mice died, with the third showing no outward evidence of toxicity at 24 hr.

As we catalog and expand databases with hundreds of novel venom peptides in each of several of the most commonly seen families of toxins found in snake venoms it becomes apparent that our understanding of novel bioactivities has become less common than our recognition of the sequences of the peptides that are found in a venom. In some cases, toxins are considered to be described prior to assays and understanding of the mechanisms that can lead to novel characteristics and traits in apparently conserved peptides. When there are large differences in sequences, the differences in function are unsurprising. However, variations that occur in bioactivity that coincide without obvious gross variation in sequence, and coincide with quaternary differences, with further study, might elucidate a novel mechanism of action.

Advances in toxicology have led to recognition of toxin family variability, but by assaying venoms thought to be quite similar, we may be able to distinguish variations in bioactivity that has great advantage to those most interested in identifying not how much they can vary a biological activity, but how to alter bioactivities with minimal structural variability.
