div.head: Introduction
div.p: Bioprospecting of the neurotoxic ligands found in elapids was instrumental to understanding neural physiology, developing novel mechanisms of research, and replicating physiological effects of other substances. These results include some with potential applications to pharmaceutical development of protein ligands. Elucidating these structural and mechanistic properties could inspire novel methods of effecting both natural and synthetic peptide or protein affinities. Quaternary modifications, such as dimerization of α-neurotoxins, may lead to unique pharmacological effects that could potentially enhance desirable bioactivities or eliminate pathophysiological bioactivities when incorporated into protein-based pharmaceuticals (Davenport et al., 2020;Ma et al., 2020).

The-3FTx has played a crucial role in understanding protein ligands, particularly through experiments involving neuromuscular and intraneuronal junction variants and subtypes. Αlphacobratoxin, an elapid α-neurotoxin, and cholinergic agonists of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR), were used in conjunction with preparations of muscles and the innervating motor neurons to determine that the post-synaptic binding to cholinergic neurotransmitter receptors by α-cobratoxin was the mechanism behind the paralysis of peripheral skeletal muscles (Gaydukov et al., 2014). Because of the selectivity of α-neurotoxins, different tissues, muscles, post-synaptic neurons, and samples of tissue serving the same physiological roles from different taxa have all been differentially susceptible or resistant to that inhibition of signal transduction. Since they also share a conserved tertiary scaffold, α-neurotoxins seem to be uniquely suited to studying identifiable compositional variables and their impacts on functional pharmacological properties.

Conventional α-neurotoxins, such as α-cobratoxin, contain four disulphide bonds and typically induce paralysis as a result of their affinity with the post-synaptic nAChRs. αcobratoxin's competitive antagonism of skeletal muscle nAChRs (α12βγδ receptors) and steric hinderance of the complexed sodium channel results in flaccid paralysis of the impacted muscle.

Non-conventional elapid α-neurotoxins often have five disulphide bonds and higher affinities for inter-neuronal nAChRs. The contrasting affinities allowed the identification, isolation, and discrimination of heptapentameric receptor complexes (Osipov et al., 2008). Research on dimeric α-neurotoxins led to identification of a tertiary variation, a disulfide within the second finger, whose presence increases the affinity towards neuromuscular receptors while eliminating the affinity towards an interneuronal receptor subtype (α7) (Osipov et al., 2008;Osipov et al., 2012;Roy et al., 2010). Novel receptor subtypes antagonized by α-neurotoxins are still being recognized (Changeux, 2012;Foo et al., 2020;Tsetlin, 2015;Utkin, 2019;Xu et al., 2011).

The neurophysiological contributions toward understanding mechanisms of neurotransmission have all been due to study of elapid venoms, despite the abundance of αneurotoxins in non-front-fanged venomous snake (NFFVS) venoms (Fry et al., 2003). Lumsden et al. (2004) evaluated many NFFVS venoms with methods that demonstrated the abundance and potency of α-neurotoxins among non-elapid venoms. The inclusion of appraisals for α-neurotoxic activity via avian biventer cervicis preparations made it one of the first to demonstrate the previously unrecognized abundance of diverse and effective α-neurotoxins within NFFVS venoms. Practical evaluations of mechanistic variations between NFFVS αneurotoxins, however, are extremely rare. This may be due to a trend where novel NFFVS αneurotoxins are presumed to be functionally identical to those that have already been evaluated (Weinstein et al., 2002). Many novel elapid α-neurotoxins are still evaluated to a depth that exceeds any research devoted to a NFFVS α-neurotoxin (Utkin, 2019; also see Pawlak et al., 2009).

The NFFVS α-neurotoxins are considered non-conventional α-neurotoxins (a naming system established prior to identification of α-neurotoxins outside the medically significant elapid venoms) for their structural resemblance to the non-conventional elapid toxins, which contain five disulfides and lack medical significance produced by inhibition of mammalian neuromuscular junctions. Outside of mammals, however, non-conventional NFFVS toxins are recognized as effectors that induce paralysis through the same mechanism as conventional αneurotoxins of elapids: the inhibition of α12βγδ. Though they deviate from non-conventional elapid α neurotoxins in this way, their affinities for the non-neuromuscular subtypes of acetylcholine receptors are mostly unexplored in any NFFVS toxin. (Lumsden et al., 2004;McIntosh et al., 2009;Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009;Saviola et al., 2014). Multiple speculations about the mechanistic cause of the taxon specificity exist, though none have been pursued in a way that elucidates that mechanism. Some examples of those speculated but not elucidated mechanisms include substitutions of amino acids that create shifts in electrostatic interactions (Harris & Fry, 2021), and sequence variations in the second finger of the toxin (Modahl, Mrinalini, & Mackessy, 2018). Presuming that any given NFFVS α-neurotoxin provokes the responses it does due to these mechanisms is similar to the same presumptions that led Lumsden et al. (2004) to conclude that NFFVS α-neurotoxins were not only common and diverse in NFFVS, but just as potent as any elapid α-neurotoxins, based on their chick biventer efficacies.

Chick biventer cervicis models were used to evaluate 16 rear-fanged snake species' venom across Colubridae, Dipsadinae, and Natricinae, revealing potent α-neurotoxicity in seven species with three-finger toxins, including three species of Boiga (Pawlak et al., 2006).

Evaluations of those α-neurotoxins from NFFVS, with the exception of sulmotoxin 1 (Modahl & Mackessy, 2019), are described as specific to avian, avian and lizard, or avian and lizard postsynaptic muscle type acetylcholine receptors (Lumsden et al., 2005;Mackessy et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009).

Appraisals of venoms extracted from a variety of colubrid, natricine, and dipsadine species first studied only recently were evaluated by Weinstein et al. (2002) with the goal of discriminating their practical threat towards humans. Because transcriptomic analyses are prevalent, while low yields often make practical toxicity evaluations difficult, Weinstein et al.

emphasized that presuming pharmacological impacts of a venom or toxin based on overall similarity without practical evaluations against an appropriate model can lead to false assumptions. Although no NFFVS α-neurotoxins are considered likely to cause any significant medical issues in humans following bites, most have not been studied thoroughly enough to elucidate their pharmacological mechanisms (Weinstein et al., 2002). Weinstein et al. specifically mentioned that 90% of the 3FTx from Boiga species are described and named denmotoxin-like toxins, despite none, with the exception of the covalent heterodimer irditoxin, undergoing the mechanistic evaluations that denmotoxin has (Pawlak et al., 2009).

One of the more common nomenclature techniques for membrane-bound receptor proteins, including those impacted by α-neurotoxins, recognizes a hierarchy that is defined by whether pharmacological specificity has been observed (Bylund & Enna, 2007). As a result, the shared specificity that denmotoxin and irditoxin demonstrate is often described interchangeably as an affinity for the α12βγδ receptor subtype or the α2β3, depending on both the date published and whether the authors recognized the new nomenclature as accurate. The rapid expansion of recognized ligands, including those of other toxin families such as those from marine organisms, leads to a rapidly diversifying landscape that, if anything, should make it more apparent that αneurotoxins of NFFVS would be unlikely to share identical pharmacological activities (Bourne et al., 2010). Αlpha-neurotoxins with shared affinities towards one receptor may still greatly deviate in other affinities and pharmacological effects. Multimeric 3FTx complexes in frontfanged venoms, where they have been scrutinized most heavily, demonstrate pharmacological affinities completely unique relative to their constituent monomers (Foo et al., 2020).

Evaluations of both monomeric toxins, like denmotoxin, and multimeric toxins, such as irditoxin, are limited to their affinity towards α12βγδ variants. Had they included multiple receptor subtypes, as nearly all elapid α-neurotoxin evaluations do, we may have recognized some extent of their variation (Foo et al., 2020;Tsetlin, 2015).

Modahl and Mackessy (2019) described samples of elapid and colubrid venoms that incapacitate broad ranges of prey. α-cobratoxin is a conventional elapid α-neurotoxin expressed by certain species in the genus Naja that effectively induces flaccid paralysis of lizards, birds and rodents. Isotoxins sulmotoxin 1 and sulditoxin are both expressed in the venom of the NFFVS Spilotes sulphureus, and are effective against mammals and lizards, respectively. Both the presence of a single non-taxon-specific toxin or multiple toxins with narrower ranges of specificity can be effective mechanisms for creating a broadly effective venom (Weinstein et al., 2002). Given the vast number of unstudied NFFVS venoms, as well as this example of the potential breadth of specificities, should cause hesitation before presuming that their venoms are exclusively toxic to non-mammalian species.
Research by Calvete et al. (2020) described an example where the taxon specificity first described was inaccurate due to the assumption that efficacies would not deviate within clades.

A toxin originally described as more toxic to Aves than squamates exhibited a more potent effect on the Green Iguana than the model squamate first used to evaluate toxicity. Calvete et al. posed an explanation that seems no more well supported than the conclusion that the venom was more specific to Aves than squamates when positing that selective adaptation of the venom to facilitate incapacitation of Iguana iguana is responsible for his observations. Evaluating multiple squamates and determining the degree, and consistency, to which they deviate in their susceptibility to various NFFVS α neurotoxins seems essential to recognizing whether the variability is the result of natural resistance in one model organism relative to another as well as whether the model organisms might deviate enough to demonstrate a degree of taxon-specific toxicity that was previously described as either toxic or non-toxic to mammal, squamate, and avian clades without analysis of variability within those groups. Two common model lizards used in toxicity trials are invasive to Guam, as are Boiga irregularis themselves, though Anolis and Hemidactylus frenatus have been recorded in dietary analyses of B. irregularis on Guam since prior to 1990 (Savidge, 1988).

Irditoxin and denmotoxin are among the most well-studied NFFVS α-neurotoxins, both of which were evaluated through x-ray chrystallography, lethal toxicity assays and ex vivo neuromuscular preparations, as well as tested on mammal, avian, and squamate models. Saviola et al. ( 2014) described the novelty and potential utility of the incomplete and reversible paralysis induced by NFFVS α-neurotoxins in mouse hemidiaphragm preparations. Reduced strength of toxin treated indirectly stimulated muscle twitches can be recovered by the introduction of cholinergic mimetics even at high toxin doses, while effective elapid α-neurotoxins elicit weakness and paralysis that is irreversible in spite of introduction of competitive agonists (Pawlak et al., 2006;Pawlak et al., 2009). During evaluations of non-conventional 3FTx from front-fanged snake's venoms, recombinant proteins that differ from natively expressed venom proteins as a result of stabilizing mutations, purification tags, or variations in glycosylation patterns have been noted; yet rarely sufficient native toxin or ligand or recombinant proteins to provide the basis for structural models (Lyukmanova et al., 2015).

Denmotoxin is a flagship and namesake of all denmotoxin-like α-neurotoxins, and irditoxin was the first heterodimeric α-neurotoxin described. Both are considered among the most well studied NFFVS α neurotoxins. But we already have seen inaccurate assumptions about NFFVS α-neurotoxins following more extensive practical evaluations. This research presents the previously undescribed variability between the effects of irditoxin, denmotoxin, and the T.

Additionally, the properties that make elapid multimeric α-neurotoxins desirable research subjects also seem evident in these NFFVS toxins. Lack of righting response was tested when breathing could be observed but when only lethargic and erratic/sluggish movements were observed. The subject was gently placed in the center of the hand on their dorsal side; if no attempt was observed after 10 s, lizards were gently stimulated with a touch. div.head: Isolation and Purification of Trimorphodon Lambda Three-Finger Toxin Dimer
div.p: As detailed in Chapter II, two bands were apparent following SDS-PAGE (see Figure 3.4), both under reducing and non-reducing conditions, of the aggregated material in the second SE chromatography peak of T. lambda venom. One band was of consistent size under both conditions, which was the same band seen following reverse phase HPLC and containing phospholipase A2 activity, as expected of the previously identified trimorphin (Huang & Mackessy, 2004). The only other obvious component on both SDS-PAGE and reverse phase chromatography was a covalently dimeric 3FTx, producing a single larger mass band under unreducing SDS-PAGE, and under reducing conditions, a single band at a mass between 6-8 kD was observed, while the higher mass band was absent. MALDI-TOF MS and MS/MS confirmed the masses of Irditoxin and the 3FTx multimer found in T. lambda as the only multimeric 3FTx observed in either venom. Sequences were confirmed by use of MS/MS (performed by Dr.

Anthony Saviola), which confirmed that the best match by spectral count and sequence identity were denmotoxin and irditoxin sequences, respectively, and that lambditoxin contained expected sequence from the transcriptomic analysis of Trimorphodon lambda 3FTx (Saviola et al., 2014;see Figures 3.4 and 3.5). The sequences of all four toxins share similar conserved regions, specifically the CYTLY and WAVK regions, though these regions are separated by a region of conserved length between denmotoxin, irditoxin A and irditoxin B, with 2 variable amino acids. Worth noting is that among the avian selective toxins, the CYLTLY and WAVK regions are conserved. The exception among rear-fanged 3FTx is the sequence of the first mammal specific 3FTx observed in rear fanged snake venoms, sulmotoxin 1, where a substitution of alanine for threonine in the WAVK region and deletion of four of the intervening residues accompany are unique among NFFVS (Mackessy, 2021). The only amino acids to vary in this conserved region between the B subunit of irditoxin and denmotoxin are shown in Figure 11. One is located immediately following the CYTLY, where irditoxin's A subunit and denmotoxin both express the acidic amino acid glutamic acid while irditoxin's B subunit and lambditoxin express the small nonpolar glycine. These are two of the most highly conserved regions in colubrid 3FTx (Modahl & Mackessy, 2019) and are located at regions similar to motifs recognized as functional domains in elapid non-conventional neurotoxins (Lyukmanova et al., 2015).

div.head: Irditoxin Purification and Separation of Subunits
div.p: In line with prior literature, the SE peak fractions generate a nearly pure preparation when analyzed by RP-HPLC. Easily discerned by the pattern produced under reducing conditions on a bis-tris SDS-PAGE, this product produced two non-overlapping 6-8 kd bands as expected (see Figure 3.6). The 60 mg of crude venom yielded 12.79 mg protein following SE chromatography. Following lyophilization of reverse phase chromatography of SE fractions, just over 5.5 mg of purified irditoxin was obtained (see Figure 3.7). The SDS-PAGE analysis of 4 μg samples in 10 uL of 1x LDS with DTT for controlled duration at a controlled incubation temperature prior to electrophoresis produced only two lower mass bands (~6 and 8 kD) at concentrations equal to or above 0.25 mM DTT but produced a sample with three bands visible (addition of high mass band at ~17 kd) at 0.125 mM DTT, and only the high mass band under control conditions when incubated without any reducing agent present. Thus, a covalent heterodimeric toxin with reduced and unreduced masses consistent with the irditoxin values was successfully isolated (Pawlak et al., 2009).

div.head: Denmotoxin and Irditoxin Monomer Reduction and Refolding
div.p: Following reduction, denmotoxin produced a single peak eluting significantly later than the native toxin. Refolding produced ~50% mass recovery relative to the quantity placed in the refolding buffer and loaded onto the HPLC after slow incubation. This was fairly consistent with the masses recovered during reverse phase of the SE peak containing native irditoxin, which yields about a 50% recovery relative to the mass of material loaded onto the Jupiter C18 column (see Figures 3.9 and 3.10). Irditoxin has no native monomers and, therefore, no known elution point for unreduced A or B monomers; however, previous observations demonstrated that reduced 3FTx eluted later, with a 5% difference in elution of the native/refolded and reduced conformations of denmotoxin.

Irditoxin's A subunit was extremely difficult to solubilize after isolation and precipitated out of solution when incubated in the cool refolding solution. The quantity of recoverable material from the protocol producing denmotoxin's refolded conformation or irditoxin subunit B's only observably bioactive refolding product was insufficient to conduct any toxicity testing. Refolding methods that allowed recovery of a realistic quantity of soluble subunit A were not bioactive in either model organism at up to 25 µg/g.

Irditoxin subunit A is the latest eluting reduced 3FTx relative to the B subunit and denmotoxin, with irditoxin's B subunit eluting at 35% B and A subunit at 42.5% B on the same gradient protocol. It is possible that the more hydrophilic B subunit facilitates solubility of the complex formed with the A monomer that is significantly higher at physiological conditions than the restrictive solubility observed with the A subunit.

Irditoxin B subunit produced a low recoverable yield (~250 μg out of 750 μg) that produced a peak with a non-uniform plateau that never approached resolving a baseline. This covers a relative change in gradient spanning 30% and 35%, a point ending at the same point as reduced subunit B elutes and beginning at a similar relative deviation as denmotoxin's refolded conformation relative to the fully reduced conformation. See figure This suggests that far more than a single refolded and non-refolded conformation is present and all material had to be combined since no cutoff point between various elutions of any single conformation was evident.

Therefore, contrasts between relative potency of the bioactive B monomer conformation and another toxin are impossible but both the presence of a bioactive conformation, a neurotoxic conformation, and relative toxicities of the B subunit towards the two model squamates (and any deviations in the ratios of effective and lethal doses both within and between the two squamates) allow for the specificity of "bioactive conformation or conformations of the B subunit" to be evaluated (see Figure 3.11).

div.head: LD50 Determinations
div.p: Righting response EC50 and LD50 of native irditoxin demonstrated potent and similar responses. The LD50 in Anolis sp. was 0.75 µg/g and 0.72 µg/g in Hemidactylus, with identical responses apart from one subject dying at the 0.5 µg/g treatment group of Hemidactylus while all survived in the Anolis group. However, the loss of righting response was >0.5 µg/g for both species, with all but a single Hemidactylus unable to right itself after 24 hr following a 0.5 µg/g injection. No loss of righting response or lethality was observed following the reduction of irditoxin when up to 25 µg/g of either both monomers or isolated monomers A and B without refolding. Triplicate evaluations of up to 10 µg/g for each were conducted prior to single 25 µg/g boluses.
Native denmotoxin differentially impacted Anolis sp. and Hemidactylus frenatus.

Triplicate treatments at 0.5, 1, 2.5, and 5 µg/g in Anolis sp. produced an EC50 comparable to irditoxin's lethal dose at 0.56 µg/g. The LD50 did not follow inhibition of righting as closely as irditoxin's lethal dose, and the LD50 of denmotoxin in Anolis sp. was 2.05 µg/g. Following reduction with DTT, no effects were observed at 25 µg/g. After the reduced denmotoxin was treated with the refolding technique, the EC50 produced in Anolis sp. after treatments of 1 µg/g, 2.5 µg/g and 5 µg/g was 1 µg/g, while the LD50 was 2.8 µg/g, with some, but relatively little loss of potency relative to native toxin. At no point was any dose of denmotoxin sufficient to produce any loss of righting response, nor lethal response, in any Hemidactylus frenatus treated in triplicate with native toxin at 5 µg/g, 10 µg/g, 15 µg/g, and a single injection of 25 µg/g. The relative toxicity of T. lambda venom was described in Chapter II. Isolated lambditoxin, the dimeric 3FTx isolated from that venom, showed no evidence of being able to induce neurotoxic effects in rats based on the lack of neurotoxic response to doses far higher than those where neurotoxic responses were seen in our squamate models. Isolated lambditoxin had an EC50 in Hemidactylus frenatus of 1.9 µg/g and an LD50 of 2.4. Anolis were moderately more tolerant with an EC50 of 2.5 µg/g and an LD50 of 3.2. It is interesting to note that the ranges between loss of righting and lethality were far greater for the monomeric proteins with toxic effects, and that the two toxins which did not impact one of the two models were both monomeric while the two dimeric conformations were mildly variable in their potency but effective against both organisms. This remains true even when considering that one of the monomeric toxic proteins evaluated is a constituent monomer of the most potent of all toxins evaluated.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Many promising natural and synthetic molecules are those ligands whose specificities are biased towards receptors through structural and functional variables not yet elucidated from similar compounds with different pharmacological affinities. Interferons, for example, function through identical mechanisms that impact the same ligand receptors and which are also uniquely biased to cause greater deleterious effects to pathogenic cells or cells infected with a viral pathogen (Kirby et al., 2021). Elucidating, and hopefully replicating, these and similar properties will require the scrutiny of biological effects and refining our comprehension of their structural and mechanistic origins. Dias et al. (2012) provided a review of how to discriminate promising and less promising bioprospecting candidate organisms and molecules. Though their review was on metabolomics, it seems equally advisable that any bioprospecting candidate would be more promising when it strikes a balance between novelty and similarity to known sources of bioprospecting utility.

Should the same advice be extrapolated to venomous sources, the ideal candidate would be one as taxonomically distinct from the best researched organisms that still produces the protein of interest, provided that this protein demonstrates evidence of distinct bioactivities. Dias et al.

further clarified that the most promising reservoirs would be those that may contain overlooked bioactive components or components with overlooked bioactivity. Combined with the emerging interest in prospecting novel applications of elucidated mechanisms that impact the specificity bias of receptor ligands, NFFVS α-neurotoxins appear to be nearly ideal.

The determination of whether or not the variation in the toxin and the receptors of the model organisms suspected binding domain for the assumed mechanism on avian/squamate muscle type acetylcholine receptor would be a prudent step in evaluating whether further mechanistic variabilities between NFFVS toxins are potentially a factor. Whether the taxonomic specificity of NFFVS α-neurotoxins is dependent on the conserved CYTLY and WAVK regions of bird/squamate specific toxins could be evaluated through site-directed mutagenesis (Heyborne & Mackessy, 2013). However, the use of synthetic peptides mimicking multiple known ligand regions of three-finger alpha neurotoxins would allow discrimination of the relative affinities for many known ligands of three finger toxins, as well as facilitating introduction of both the actual sequences, and the impact of any substitutions before using an organismal model (Kudryavtsev et al., 2020). Modahl, Mrinalini, and Mackessy (2018) speculated that the sequence substitutions observed in sulmotoxin 1, threonine => asparagine (CYTLY to CYNLY) and an alanine => threonine (WAVK to WTVK) substitutions respectively, are likely relevant to the unique mammal-specific toxicity of the toxin. Similarly, site-directed mutagenesis could also replicate the shortening of the loop II sequence observed in sulmotoxin 1and conventional αneurotoxins, another trait speculated to be influential to taxon specificity. The sequences of all four toxins share similar conserved regions, specifically the CYTLY and WAVK regions.

However, the amino acid which is not conserved varies between two amino acids which have one of the greatest potential impacts that any single substitution makes to the sequence of a binding domain. Glutamic acid is expressed by the irditoxin A subunit and denmotoxin, while in both the B subunit of irditoxin and lambditoxin, glycine is expressed. As a result of the impact that replacing a small, non-polar glycine with a large, ionized (under physiological pH) glutamic acid, one could anticipate extremely significant variations in the relative affinity to a particular binding region associated with it and the residues in the immediate vicinity. Thus, while this is one of many possible explanations, it is not as unreasonable an explanation for such extreme variations in toxicity produced due to a substitution. Determining the sequence of the corresponding receptor for Hemidactylus frenatus would allow further speculation and evaluation including other toxins evaluated on these models. While not necessarily feasible due to the unpredictability of refolding proteins, it would be very interesting to determine whether the A subunit of irditoxin might have the opposite effect on the two model organisms as the B subunit regarding efficacy and tolerance. Expressing both a binding domain with and without a growth of the industry. The other factor was the introduction of unnatural amino acids, such as those with enantiomeric residues relative to natural amino acids.

Modifications to pharmaceutical human glucagon (GLP-1) agonists, first sourced from Heloderma suspectum venom and discussed in Chapter I, are considered by Davenport et al. (2020) to be indicative of the types of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic improvements stemming from chemical modifications whose recognition should be considered equally valuable products of bioprospecting as any other. Replacing an existing amino acid with a lysine, a glycosylated side group, an unnatural enantiomer of lysine, all decreased efficacy of natural enzymes, and each slowed the metabolic breakdown more than the prior modification. Covalent dimerization, as well as fusion with certain protein domains both increase the affinity for serum albumen. This affinity serves to both avoid enzymatic breakdown and provide an extended duration of stable plasma levels of the drug. Though the original mechanism of stimulating GLP-1 receptors has remained unaltered, the introduced structural and chemical modifications each led to a more effective drug, providing more reliable efficacy and decreasing the number of injections a patient requires (Davenport et al., 2020). Dimerization of conotoxins proved beneficial in ziconotide-like pharmaceuticals as well, potentially aiding in permeability (Liang et al., 2020).

Studying as many peptide/receptor interactions as possible provides the greatest chance of elucidating the variable mechanisms that allow similarly structured proteins to have, as irditoxin B and denmotoxin demonstrated, opposite efficacies on either Anolis or Hemidactylus lizards while producing no observable toxic effects in the other. Dimerizations that form complexes that may aid in predictably modifying proteins in such a way that desirable specificities of constituent monomers are preserved or enhanced, while undesirable affinities are avoided or suppressed, are of undeniable value.

The application of a mechanism observed through such study of a natural toxin, such as NFFVS toxins, is made very explicit as the developers of a synthetic therapeutic laud the impact that research on a scorpion toxin has had on their progress. The 0GF β interacts with a colorectal metastatic cancer to promote production of the protein coded for by an oncogene that significantly increases the metastatic growth of said cancer. A TGF β inhibitor synthetically produced as a small peptide effectively inhibits metastases but unfortunately lacks the selectivity bias necessary to limit the effects on the TGF β modulated wound healing and stem cell propagation in healthy physiological pathways. Research published by Ma et al. (2020) lauded the venoms, especially those regions and combinations of binding domains that have remained mostly conserved after hundreds of thousands of years of evolution, are stable, reliable, and often produce effects that maximize specificity in ways that we have not yet considered. They then elaborate on the efficacy of their most recent synthetic product after dimerization of the first with a small peptide whose affinity for a ligand unlikely to be expressed alongside TGF β ligands on non-cancerous cells has reduced deleterious effects without loss of antimetastatic effects.
The results of the toxicity evaluations of the monomeric and dimeric bioactive neurotoxins demonstrated in this research revealed that both dimeric complexes were toxic to

Anolis and Hemidactylus at approximately identical doses. The monomeric proteins evaluated both induced toxic effects in either Anolis or Hemidactylus while failing to produce any evidence of toxicity in the other organism. Furthermore, denmotoxin and irditoxin's B monomer were selectively toxic to opposite model organisms, suggesting that neither model organism was truly resistant to the paralytic mechanisms of NFFVS α-neurotoxins. However, the cause behind these differences may depend on distribution, metabolic breakdown, or their receptor interactions. Xray crystallography and evaluation of affinities towards receptor variants are what Davenport et al. (2020) believed that basic peptide-receptor structure-activity relationships, the foundation of any project intended to intentionally design a molecule to perform a function, might begin to be realized only after we understand how those that already exist perform those functions. The identification of endogenous human regulatory proteins with 3FTx-like motifs, such as Lys 6 and the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor, suggest that identification of mechanisms that can be reproduced in other three finger motifs might have practical utility (Bufalo et al., 2014).

Combined with their shared affinities for the same family of acetylcholine receptor, and even overlapping specificities for particular subtypes within that family, and that certain endogenous Lys6/uPAR proteins, specifically SLURP-1 and SLURP-2, have paracrine impacts on swelling and cell proliferation that may inhibit tumor growth, discriminating structure-function mechanisms on snake venom 3FTx have far more promising potential utilities if they can be translated to any protein with a three finger motif (Lyukmanova et al., 2010). As Ma et al. (2020) described, one of the greatest benefits provided by working with venom proteins is that they represent a massive variety of proteins which evolved to produce similar, but not identical, pharmacological profiles.

Other multimeric complexes in venoms are recognized as composed of non-toxic and mildly toxic components that, when complexed, decrease the affinity for nonspecific binding to an abundant ligand and saturate the effector of the most deleterious physiological symptoms at doses magnitudes below what even the more toxic of the two monomers could produce without dimerization (Georgieva et al., 2016). The irditoxin A subunit may, therefore, facilitate a similar shuttling effect whose hydrophobicity is unrelated to the efficacy of the mechanism. We can only speculate at this point, though we can acknowledge that selective, mechanistic, pharmacokinetic, or pharmacodynamic variations exist between NFFVS α-neurotoxins than can be defined as selective affinities for avian and squamate neuromuscular junctions.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: The understudied condition of rear-fanged snake venoms is well recognized. Few are surprised to learn that under 3%-5% of an indeterminate number of venomous rear-fanged species were to any extent. However, there is another knowledge gap which may be more impactful on the relative lack of venoms inform pharmaceutical designs relative to the exponentially greater quantity of bioactive toxin peptides to consider. Many herpetologists are toxicologists, ecologists, and evolutionary biologists but, as quoted earlier (Chapter I) "in venoms, we find what only what we look for," than perhaps the results of this thesis highlight how few of those studying novel snake venoms are looking for structure-function relationships that are both the ultimate outcome of all toxin variability, and also that define the databases that would be most directly relevant to pharmaceutical peptide design.

This research demonstrates that sequencing every peptide and mRNA transcript found in a Duvernoy's venom gland and venom fail to support conclusions drawn after practical evaluations outside typical venomic workflows are introduced.

Trimorphodon lambda and Philodryas baroni both expressed previously unrecognized multimeric toxins (Chapter II). The P. baroni demonstrated highly potent metalloproteases, one that is potentially a dimeric metalloprotease, and one containing C-type lectin domains (Chapter II).

In the 20 years since the first recognition of rear-fanged -neurotoxins, there have been few studies to clarify the extent of their recognized taxon specificity. These toxins are almost exclusively referred to collectively as selective antagonists of avian and squamate muscle type acetylcholine receptors (a collective grouping that is often not even evaluated when a novel toxin is sequenced). The inclusion of an additional squamate in the toxicity analysis of two of the most well recognized of the rear-fanged alpha neurotoxins, including the namesake of all denmotoxin like toxins, reveals that they are more diverse than previously described (Chapter III).

Furthermore, potential impacts of dimerization on specificity of irditoxin was never evaluated beyond the assays that were used to determine that denmotoxin, and thus all denmotoxin-like toxins, were specifically toxic to birds and lizards.

This impact was evaluated (Chapter III) by using two models and the relative toxic and lethal doses for each dimeric and monomeric toxin evaluated. As the two most common models on which nearly all rear-fanged venom lizard-specific activities are based, Anolis sp. and Hemidactylus frenatus would seem to be the two species that would most likely have been contrasted to determine whether their uses in analyses evaluating the same characteristic introduced variability which was not taken into account when comparing multiple studies.
Not only was irditoxin specificity distinct from denmotoxin specificity, but Hemidactylus frenatus are completely unaffected by denmotoxin, which is highly lethal to Anolis sp.

Furthermore, the B subunit of irditoxin, when bioactive following isolation and refolding, was toxic only to Hemidactylus frenatus, exhibiting the opposite overall specificity as denmotoxin and distinct from native irditoxin, equally toxic to both Anolis sp. and Hemidactylus frenatus (Chapter III).

The T. lambda's toxin sequence was not only present in alpha neurotoxin transcriptomic databases, but that sequence has been used to exemplify an unpaired cysteine found within a monomeric three-finger toxin (3FTx); in actuality, those cysteines pair with those of another molecule to form the covalent homodimer described throughout this research as lambditoxin.

Neither after appearing in transcriptomics as potentially capable of dimerizing, nor when observed as a novelty among monomeric toxins was it considered that banding was present at the locations that would obscure those revealing a dimeric 3FTx's presence under both reducing and non-reducing conditions. Partial isolation of constituent proteins found within the whole by size exclusion (SE) chromatography produced distinct peaks, two of which contained proteins with banding patterns identical under non-reducing conditions, one of a non-dimeric protein, and multiple peaks with monomeric 3FTx under reducing and non-reducing conditions, and one without 3FTx monomers under non-reduced conditions. The migrating band in the second SE peak revealed the presence and allowed isolation of the dimeric three finger toxin, as well as reveals why it would be overlooked despite comparison of reduced and non-reduced T. lambda venom in past studies. This toxin appears to play a significant role in the efficacy of T. lambda crude venom to incapacitate lizards at a dose 10 times lower than necessary to eventually induce fatalities in mice, and no evidence suggesting neurotoxicity in those mice exposed (Chapter II).

The relatively recent recognition of endogenous regulatory proteins with three fingermotifs (ly6 type proteins) including SLURP-1 and SLURP-2 with roles in human would healing, cell proliferation, and mediation of the same family of acetylcholine receptors that snake venom alpha neurotoxins antagonize makes the practicality that identifying mechanisms that alter pharmacological specificities and relative affinities for the ligands of their respective 3Finger protein motifs seem far more potentially applicable for producing effects other than more or less effective neurotoxicity than when observed primarily in snake venom proteins. Particularly quaternary deviations whose mechanisms might potentially translate when replicated in other proteins with similar motifs. The venomic analyses were, in fact, highly useful in identifying the isolated toxins, particularly the dimeric alpha neurotoxin from T. lambda venom (Chapters II and III). This highlights the need for broader evaluation of novel venoms, as well as previously evaluated rear-fanged snake venoms. Transcriptomic and rapid sequencing analyses are going to reveal far more of the variability between any two species of venomous snakes, as the number of covalently bound multimeric toxins are relatively few compared to the total number of proteins in a venom and the ways that such massive shifts in the steric, mass, and overall physical properties of a protein will still produce quaternary deviations that aren't eliminated by selective pressures, particularly if shifts in bioactivity without a corresponding shift in composition of proteome is observed. As well as when the unexpected presence of unpaired cysteines is a novelty among a certain toxin family, there is sufficient reason to recognize that those exploring novel methods of synthesizing proteins with bioactivity against potentially useful ligands often lack the appropriate selectivity, affinity, or other pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic attributes. In such cases the nearly limitless variations between sequence and mechanism become nearly as overwhelming as random sequence variation, while quaternary structure deviations with particular effects on a particular characteristic of that protein might be a more easily translated and recognizable potential method for improving the efficacy of that biologic, biomimetic, or synthetic pharmaceutical candidate.
